text:
SOPs can now be turned into workflows. Experience can be turned into skills. And once that happens, "years of experience" becomes a pretty weak metric. Someone might have 20 years under their belt, but in reality, it’s often just the same 5 to 10 operating loops repeated across different projects, tools, and companies. Which brings up an uncomfortable question: What’s the value of the traditional corporate soldier? In a lot of companies, it’s no longer about pure execution, coordination, sign-offs, reporting, or escalating. That stuff is getting codified, automated, or straight-up handled by AI. Real value is shifting toward judgment, exception handling, accountability, context, and the ability to build new solutions on the fly when the SOP breaks down. But that’s not how organizations actually reward people. In practice, the ultimate "survival skill" is keeping the recipe secret.

Limit data access. Skip the documentation. Make sure only a handful of people know how to handle the edge cases. Create dependency.

When knowledge becomes a workflow and experience becomes a skill, information asymmetry turns into job security. The person who documents, teaches, automates, and removes bottlenecks might just make themselves irrelevant. The person who protects the bottleneck gets more authority, bigger headcount, and better job security. That’s the tragic part. The employee who fixes the system might automate themselves right out of a job. The employee who keeps the system dependent on them gets promoted for "managing" the complexity they created. The playing field was never fair. But secrecy is just a defensive moat. It protects yesterday’s value. The real long-term flex is becoming the person who continuously creates new value: Spotting new problems, building new workflows, redesigning broken processes, navigating ambiguity, and owning the outcomes. Knowledge hoarding makes you hard to replace. Capability building makes you impossible to ignore.
